bib.title: The Relation between Adversarial and Stochastic Linear Bandits (Bandit Algorithms, ch. 29)

question: How do adversarial and stochastic linear bandits relate, and why do their regret bounds on the unit ball differ (O(sqrt(dn log n)) vs Omega(d sqrt n))?
contributions: A unified loss notation for the stochastic and adversarial settings
A reduction from stochastic to adversarial linear bandits via an augmented action set
Parameter-noise stochastic linear bandits as the model the adversarial one really relaxes, explaining the unit-ball gap
Discussion of why regret for changing action sets (contextual) is unresolved in the adversarial setting

results.claim: Stochastic linear bandit regret is bounded by the adversarial bound B_n when the adversarial policy is run on the augmented action set A_aug={(a,1)} with adversary theta_t=(theta,eta_t); the reduction needs |<a,theta>+eta_t|<=1 a.s.
results.setup: Fixed action set A in R^d, reduction of Section 29.2; algorithm run on d+1 dimensions.
results.quote: Therefore, the expected regret in the stochastic bandit is also at most Bn.

results.claim: The augmentation changes the geometry: for the unit ball neither A_aug nor the dual loss set is a unit ball, so the adversary becomes more powerful, consistent with the Omega(d sqrt n) stochastic lower bound.
results.quote: we see that the changed geometry must make the adversary more powerful.

results.claim: Variance of the induced noise in parameter-noise bandits depends on the action: V_t = A_t' Sigma A_t, so long actions are noisier; for Gaussian nu with identity covariance it is ||A_t||_2^2.
results.setup: theta_t iid from nu with mean theta and covariance Sigma.
results.quote: the noise variance scales with the length of At.

results.claim: Under uniform play on the sphere with nu on the unit sphere, expected predictable noise variance is 1/d, versus 1 in the standard 1-subgaussian model, which explains the sqrt(d) gap between ~O(sqrt(dn)) adversarial and ~O(d sqrt n) stochastic regret.
results.setup: A_t drawn from uniform measure mu on the unit sphere; nu supported on the unit sphere (eigenvalues of Sigma sum to one).

results.claim: If the adversary may choose loss vectors from the sphere of radius sqrt(d), predictable variation is 1 and regret scales linearly in d, matching the vanilla stochastic case.
results.quote: would scale linearly in d, which also matches the vanilla stochastic case.

results.claim: The standard adversarial linear model generalises the parameter-noise stochastic model; parameter noise can be easier because it limits the adversary's control of signal-to-noise ratio.
results.quote: generalises the stochastic linear bandit with parameter noise.

results.claim: Parameter-noise stochastic bandits reduce trivially to adversarial bandits when Supp(nu) is bounded, with no change to the action set.

results.claim: In the stochastic contextual setting LinUCB has regret ~O(d sqrt n) against the per-round optimal action; no algorithm is known with small regret against the analogous adversarial benchmark R_n(Theta) for continuous Theta.
results.quote: we do not currently know how to design algorithms for which this regret is small.

results.claim: For finite Theta the Chapter 27 techniques give O(sqrt(dn log|Theta|)) for the adversarial contextual regret, but this is computationally inefficient for large |Theta| and covering a continuous set does not give a bound against the larger set.
Running an adversarial algorithm directly on the original action set usually works for possibly-stochastic environments but may need different tuning.

results.claim: sqrt(dn) regret is impossible on a shifted unit ball A={a+x:||x||<=1}, a=(2,0,...,0) (Shamir 2015), also implied by the reduction.
results.quote: which also follows from our reduction in Section 29.2.

limits: Chapter is conceptual: no experiments, no empirical rates beyond cited theorems.
Reduction assumes bounded losses |<a,theta>+eta|<=1 and existence of the minimiser a*; Gaussian noise handled only by truncation (Note 1).
Effect of action set and adversary choices on regret is not well understood beyond l_p balls (Bibliographic Remarks).
Meaningful adversarial regret for changing action sets (contextual) is open; no efficient algorithm known.
No systematic study of parameter noise in the stochastic setting known to the authors.
practices: For a stochastic linear bandit with a fixed action set, run your favourite adversarial linear bandit algorithm on the augmented set {(a,1)} (Sec 29.2).
If unsure whether the environment is stochastic, run the adversarial algorithm on the original action set, retuned (Sec 29.2, Ex 29.2-29.3).
For changing action sets prefer stochastic algorithms such as LinUCB, since the adversarial regret notion is less meaningful (Sec 29.4).
